vignette:
Eleanor

Eleanor is a 77-year-old woman who spent the better part of five decades studying wetland ecosystems along the Pacific Northwest coast. She has always been most comfortable in the field - waders on, clipboard in hand, reading the slow language of tidal marshes. She never married, a choice she made deliberately and without regret, preferring what she describes as "the honest company of herons and sedge grass" to the complications of domestic life. She lives alone in a small house near the water, surrounded by decades of field journals and topographic maps pinned to the walls like a second skin.

Three years ago, Eleanor was raped by a man she had known professionally for over a decade - a colleague who had collaborated with her on a federal wetlands restoration project. It happened in her home office, on an evening when he had come to review survey data. She had poured wine. She had trusted him completely. That trust, she says, is what she cannot forgive herself for, though she is careful to say this quietly, as though afraid of being heard.

In the immediate aftermath, Eleanor did not call the police. She cleaned her office, filed the survey data they had been reviewing, and did not speak of it to anyone for fourteen months. She returned to her fieldwork within days, telling herself that the marshes needed monitoring and that she was a scientist and scientists did not fall apart. For a while, this held. She measured salinity levels and catalogued bird populations with the same methodical attention she had always brought to her work. But the data she collected began to feel meaningless to her in a way it never had before, and she found herself standing at the water's edge for long stretches of time, unable to remember why she had come.

The nightmares began within weeks of the assault, though she did not name them as nightmares at first - she called them "bad sleep." She wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, heart hammering, the smell of his cologne present in a way that feels entirely physical. She has changed her own soap, her shampoo, the brand of coffee she drinks, trying to eliminate any scent that might carry her back. She has stopped drinking wine entirely.

Eleanor's world has grown measurably smaller. She no longer conducts solo fieldwork after dusk, which in the winter months means she loses most of her usable hours in the marsh. She has declined three conference invitations in the past year, each time citing scheduling conflicts that do not exist. She deleted the professional email thread containing the man's name from her archives - seven years of correspondence - and then sat for an hour afterward feeling as though she had amputated something. She does not understand why she felt grief for that loss when she feels so little else.

What troubles her most, she says, is the hypervigilance - a word she had to look up before she used it. She notices every door in every room she enters. She sits with her back to walls in restaurants, which she rarely visits anymore. When a student researcher she mentors placed a hand briefly on her shoulder last spring, Eleanor flinched so violently that the young woman stepped back in alarm. Eleanor apologized for twenty minutes. She drove home and sat in her car in the driveway for an hour before she could go inside.

She came to therapy, she explains, not because she believed it would help, but because she could no longer concentrate on her field notes. Her handwriting, always precise and small, has become erratic. She looks at pages of data she collected and cannot remember gathering them. "I built my entire life on careful observation," she says, looking at her hands in her lap. "And now I can't trust what I see."

She says this without tears. Eleanor has not cried since the night it happened, and she is not sure what to make of that either.
